item.title: DLE 2026-05-26
item.description:
1. The Funny One

"States are not ruled with prayer-books." — Cosimo de' Medici

When a prospect asks if your cold outreach is "too aggressive," deploy this. Not as an argument. Just let it hang there.

2. Business Insight

A — Thiel, Zero to One: "If you've invented something new but you haven't invented an effective way to sell it, you have a bad business — no matter how good the product." Most founders treat GTM as the cleanup act after engineering. The Kiln exists because that assumption kills companies. Sell this line back to them in the first five minutes.

B — Cialdini, Influence: "Persons who go through a great deal of trouble or pain to attain something tend to value it more highly than persons who attain the same thing with a minimum of effort." A rigorous Kiln onboarding process — intake calls, tech audits, ICP workshops — isn't friction. It's perceived value manufacture. Make clients work a little before they pay you a lot.

3. Deep Line

"Think lightly of yourself and deeply of the world." — Miyamoto Musashi

The founder who stops narrating their own story long enough to actually study the customer wins. Ego is the gap between what you think your pitch says and what the prospect hears.

4. Thought Principle: The Iron Law of Oligarchy

Every organisation, no matter how flat it starts, eventually consolidates power into a small ruling group. Michels observed this in political parties; it happens identically in agency teams, client procurement committees, and VC-backed startups. The people who formally hold power are often not the people who actually move decisions.

For The Kiln: on any enterprise deal, find the person who controls the narrative in the buying group — not just the budget holder. That person is the real committee. Sell to them first.

5. New Words & Terms

Epistemic closure — the condition of a belief system that is entirely self-confirming; new evidence gets filtered out or reinterpreted to preserve existing conclusions. "The founder hadn't spoken to a customer in six months — classic epistemic closure. Every data point he encountered confirmed what he already believed about his ICP."

Prolepsis — a rhetorical device where you anticipate and address an objection before the audience raises it; from the Greek for 'anticipation'. "The best cold email Ultan ever wrote used prolepsis in the second line: 'You're probably wondering why a GTM agency is cold-emailing you about cold email — fair enough, here's why it's worth thirty seconds.'"

Regulatory capture — the process by which a regulatory agency, created to act in the public interest, instead advances the commercial or political concerns of the industry it is meant to regulate. "The committee that was supposed to evaluate vendors objectively had been regulatory-captured by the incumbent supplier; three of the five members had been wined-and-dined for two years."

6. Stoic Closer

"He who fears death will never do anything worthy of a living man." — Seneca

The pitch you're too nervous to send is the one you should have sent first.

7. Daily Math: Kelly Criterion

Concept: The Kelly Criterion is a formula for determining what fraction of your bankroll — or budget, or capacity — to allocate to a bet, given a known edge and known odds. It was derived by John Kelly at Bell Labs in 1956, originally to solve a problem in signal transmission, and immediately adopted by gamblers and later by investors (Ed Thorp used it to beat blackjack and then Wall Street).

The formula is:

f* = (bp − q) / b

Where: - f* is the fraction of your resources to allocate - b is the net odds received (i.e., you win b units per 1 unit bet) - p is the probability of winning - q is the probability of losing (q = 1 − p)

A simpler rearrangement you'll see often:

f* = p − (q / b)

Or equivalently: f* = (edge) / (odds)

The core insight: bet too small and you're leaving compounding on the table. Bet too large and a losing streak destroys you even if your edge is real. Kelly finds the mathematically optimal fraction that maximises the long-run growth rate of your stake.

Business example: Suppose The Kiln is considering two growth investments for next quarter — say, a dedicated SDR hire versus a Clay tooling upgrade — and you're trying to allocate limited capacity (time, cash, attention) between them.

Model the SDR hire: - You estimate 60% probability it meaningfully accelerates pipeline within 90 days (p = 0.60) - If it works, the return is roughly 3x the cost in new revenue within the quarter (b = 3) - If it doesn't, you've spent the salary with no return (q = 0.40)

Applying Kelly:

f* = (3 × 0.60 − 0.40) / 3 = (1.80 − 0.40) / 3 = 1.40 / 3 ≈ 0.467

Kelly says: commit roughly 47% of your available discretionary capacity to this bet. Not all of it. Not a timid 10% hedge. 47% — which feels aggressive until you compare it to the naive instinct of "go all in because it feels right."

Now model the Clay upgrade: - 80% probability of a meaningful workflow improvement (p = 0.80) - But the upside is more modest — roughly 1.5x return on the time invested (b = 1.5) - q = 0.20

f* = (1.5 × 0.80 − 0.20) / 1.5 = (1.20 − 0.20) / 1.5 = 1.00 / 1.5 ≈ 0.667

Counterintuitive result: the Clay upgrade scores higher on Kelly, not because its upside is bigger, but because the probability of success is substantially higher and the downside is lower. High certainty of a modest return often beats uncertain shots at large returns — Kelly makes this rigorous rather than merely a feeling.

Insight: Kelly answers a question that most founders never formally ask: given that I have a real edge, how much should I actually press it?

The most common error is under-betting on high-confidence, moderate-return investments (the Clay upgrade scenario) while over-betting on exciting but low-probability moonshots. Kelly rebalances this intuitively. It also does something important: it makes explicit that the size of the allocation is a function of both probability and odds — you need both numbers, which forces you to actually estimate them rather than operating on vibes.

Two practical limits worth knowing:

First, half-Kelly — betting half of what Kelly recommends — is a common conservative adjustment when you're uncertain about your probability estimate. It sacrifices roughly 25% of expected growth rate in exchange for dramatically reduced variance. Most practitioners use it in real-world conditions where p is estimated rather than known.

Second, Kelly assumes repeated independent bets with the same edge. A business doesn't quite work like that — each hire, each client, each campaign is somewhat correlated. But the framework still disciplines your thinking even when applied imperfectly.

Today's exercise: Pick one real investment decision The Kiln faces in the next 30 days — a hire, a channel, a software tool, a partnership conversation.

1. Estimate p: what's the honest probability this works within your defined time horizon? 2. Estimate b: if it works, what's the return multiple relative to the cost? 3. Calculate f* using the Kelly formula. 4. Compare that number to what you were instinctively planning to allocate.

If your gut allocation was lower than Kelly, ask why. Are you underestimating your edge? Risk-averse beyond what the numbers justify? If your gut was higher than Kelly, that's a warning sign — you're likely overconfident in p or underweighting the downside.

The goal isn't to mechanically follow the formula. It's to use it as a mirror: Kelly reveals where your conviction and your resource allocation are out of sync.

This completes the current curriculum sequence: Expected Value → Bayes' Theorem → Law of Large Numbers → Standard Deviation → Normal Distribution → Confidence Intervals → Regression to the Mean → Pareto Distribution → Conditional Probability → Monte Carlo → Markov Chains → Kelly Criterion.

item.title: DLE 2026-05-25
item.description:
1. The Funny One

"Never, ever say that you have no competitors. That signals naivete. Great markets draw competitors, and so if you really have no competition, you must not be in a great market." — Marc Andreessen

Deploy when a founder proudly tells you their pitch deck says "no one else is doing this." Smile, nod, then ask them to reconsider whether that's actually a flex.

2. Business Insight

A — Zero to One (Thiel): "Poor sales rather than bad product is the most common cause of failure." Most founders at €20k MRR are still treating sales as the thing they do after the real work. For The Kiln, the real work is the sales system — every client you build one for is proof you've solved the problem yourself.

B — Originals (Grant): "The biggest barrier to originality is not idea generation — it's idea selection." The Kiln probably has a backlog of positioning angles, offer variants, and outbound approaches it's never shipped. The constraint isn't more ideas — it's a fast, honest filter for killing the mediocre ones before they eat the calendar.

3. Deep Line

"Every great business is built around a secret that's hidden from the outside. When you share your secret, the recipient becomes a fellow conspirator." — Peter Thiel

The Kiln's secret isn't Clay or data enrichment — those are tools. The secret is that GTM infrastructure, built properly, is compounding and defensible. Every client you tell that to either gets it immediately and signs, or doesn't and wasn't your client anyway.

4. Thought Principle: Vuja De

Most people experience a market for years and never question its defaults. Vuja de is the discipline of staring at something familiar — your client's broken CRM, their dead outbound sequence, their manually-built lead list — and asking why it has to be this way at all. It's not naivety; it's structured re-examination.

For The Kiln, this means treating every new client's existing GTM stack as a crime scene rather than a starting point. The value isn't in improving what's there — it's in questioning whether what's there should exist at all.

5. New Words & Terms

Proprioception — the body's internal sense of its own position and movement, without needing to look; metaphorically, a system's ability to monitor itself from within. "The best GTM stacks have proprioception — the CRM knows when it's drifting, the sequences self-report what's working, and the whole thing doesn't need a consultant to tell it where it is."

Salient — standing out from surrounding material in a way that naturally draws attention; often used in psychology and economics to describe options or features that dominate perception disproportionately. "In a cold email, the one salient detail — a specific revenue number, a named competitor, a fresh news hook — does more work than four paragraphs of company description."

Satisficing — a portmanteau of 'satisfy' and 'suffice', coined by Herbert Simon; choosing an option that is good enough rather than optimising for the theoretical best. "Most buyers aren't maximising — they're satisficing. They want a GTM partner that clears a competence threshold and doesn't make their life harder. The Kiln's pitch should clear that bar, not dazzle them into confusion."

6. Stoic Closer

"If it is not right, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it." — Marcus Aurelius

Runs fine as a business principle too — fewer decks, fewer promises, fewer wasted Tuesdays.

7. Daily Math: Markov Chains

Concept: A Markov chain is a system that moves between a defined set of states, where the probability of transitioning to the next state depends only on the current state — not on any history of how you got there. This is called the Markov property, or more bluntly, the "memoryless" property.

Formally: if the system is in state S at time t, then the probability of being in state S' at time t+1 is fixed and depends solely on S, not on S₋₁, S₋₂, or anything before.

You define a Markov chain with: 1. A set of states (e.g., Prospect, MQL, SQL, Proposal, Closed-Won, Churned) 2. A transition matrix — a table where entry P(i,j) is the probability of moving from state i to state j in one step 3. An initial distribution — where things start

The magic is that after enough steps, many Markov chains converge to a stationary distribution: a stable long-run proportion of time spent in each state, regardless of where you started. Think of it as the system's natural resting shape.

Business example: Model a simplified Kiln sales pipeline as a Markov chain with five states:

| State | Description | |---|---| | Prospect | In outreach, not yet engaged | | Conversation | Discovery call booked or held | | Proposal | Proposal sent | | Client | Paying retainer | | Lost | Dropped out at any stage |

Now define transition probabilities (monthly):

| From \ To | Prospect | Conversation | Proposal | Client | Lost | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Prospect | 0.60 | 0.25 | 0 | 0 | 0.15 | | Conversation | 0 | 0.20 | 0.50 | 0 | 0.30 | | Proposal | 0 | 0 | 0.10 | 0.55 | 0.35 | | Client | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0.93 | 0.07 | | Lost | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1.00 |

Reading this: a Prospect has a 25% chance of booking a conversation this month, 60% chance of staying in outreach, and 15% chance of going cold. A Proposal has a 55% chance of converting to a Client.

Now ask: if you start 100 prospects in the top of the funnel, what does the system look like after 6 months? You multiply the initial state vector by the transition matrix repeatedly — the numbers flow forward through the pipeline automatically.

Insight: Two things become visible immediately when you model a pipeline as a Markov chain:

First, the conversion rate that matters most is usually not the one people obsess over. Everyone watches Proposal-to-Close. But the Markov model shows that if your Prospect-to-Conversation rate drops from 25% to 15%, the downstream Client count falls drastically even if your close rate holds. Volume at the top of the chain has enormous leverage on the final state.

Second, churn is a transition probability, and it compounds brutally. A 7% monthly churn rate sounds modest. But in steady state, the average client tenure is just 1/0.07 ≈ 14 months. Halving that churn rate to 3.5% doubles average tenure — without signing a single new client. The model makes this arithmetic unavoidable.

Markov chains also expose whether your pipeline will reach a steady state — a predictable long-run distribution across stages — or whether it will drain out over time because the "Lost" state is absorbing everything. In the example above, Lost is an absorbing state (once you're there, you stay). The only way to maintain a healthy client base is a continuous inflow of new Prospects. The model tells you the exact inflow rate required to sustain a target number of active clients.

Today's exercise: Sketch The Kiln's current pipeline as a Markov chain:

1. Define four to six states that represent where a contact actually sits in your world (not where a CRM template says they should sit). 2. Estimate, honestly, the monthly transition probabilities between each pair of states. What fraction of Prospects become Conversations each month? What fraction of Proposals close? 3. Pick one transition probability and ask: if I doubled this rate, what happens to the number of active Clients after six months?

You don't need a computer. A back-of-envelope calculation for two or three iterations reveals the shape. The insight you're after is: which single transition, if improved, has the most downstream leverage? That's the stage of your pipeline that deserves the most deliberate investment this quarter.

Next: Kelly Criterion.

item.title: DLE 2026-05-22
item.description:
1. The Funny One

"Inventing is messy, and over time, it's certain that we'll fail at some big bets too."
— Jeff Bezos, to shareholders, as a man worth $100 billion.

Deploy when someone asks how you handle failure. "As Bezos put it — and he said this after building the everything store — inventing is messy. If it's good enough for him, it's good enough for whatever I've broken this week."

2. Business Insight

A — Marc Andreessen: "In a great market, the market pulls product out of the startup." Most agencies grind at pushing services onto lukewarm ICPs. The Kiln's diagnostic question isn't "how do we close more?" — it's "are we in a market where GTM infrastructure is demanded, or are we still convincing people they need it?" If you're spending more energy justifying the category than closing deals, you may be in the wrong pond.

B — Jim Collins: "'Stop doing' lists are more important than 'to do' lists." At $20k MRR climbing toward €100k, the instinct is to add — new services, new channels, new outreach angles. But the faster lever is almost always deletion. What client type, service offering, or internal process is eating time without compounding toward the goal? Cut it before it becomes load-bearing by accident.

3. Deep Line

"It is not money that is the sinews of war, but good soldiers. For money cannot find good soldiers, but good soldiers will be sure to find money." — Machiavelli

Don't raise, borrow, or beg for resources before you've proven you can use them. Build the capability first — the capital follows execution, not the other way around.

4. Thought Principle: Vuja De

Most experienced operators miss the biggest opportunities because familiarity breeds blindness — they stop seeing what they look at every day. Vuja de is the deliberate practice of seeing the familiar as if for the first time: asking "why does this work this way?" about things everyone else has stopped questioning.

Kiln application: Look at your client's current GTM stack the way a smart outsider would — not "how do we optimise this?" but "why does anyone do it this way at all?" The highest-value infrastructure builds often come from noticing an assumption nobody has interrogated in years. The insight hiding inside the obvious default is usually worth more than the incremental improvement everyone is chasing.

5. New Words & Terms

Oligopoly — a market structure in which a small number of firms collectively dominate, each aware that its decisions affect and are affected by the others; distinguished from monopoly by the presence of a few competitors rather than one. "The GTM tooling space is drifting toward oligopoly — three or four platforms will own the infrastructure layer, and every agency will have to build on top of one of them whether they like it or not."

Concave payoff — a return profile where outcomes plateau or diminish past a certain point; the opposite of convex, where upside is unbounded. "Agency retainer work has a concave payoff — there's a ceiling on what any single client pays, which is exactly why The Kiln needs a productised offer alongside bespoke work."

Attrition rate — the percentage of customers or revenue lost over a given period, distinct from churn in that it often refers to gradual, passive losses rather than explicit cancellations. "Knowing your monthly attrition rate is more useful than knowing your churn events — it tells you what's quietly bleeding out before anyone picks up the phone to cancel."

6. Stoic Closer

"Waste no more time arguing about what a good man should be. Be one." — Marcus Aurelius

Every hour spent debating the ideal system is an hour not spent building the actual one.

7. Daily Math: Monte Carlo Simulation

Concept: A Monte Carlo simulation runs a model hundreds or thousands of times, each time sampling inputs randomly from a defined probability distribution, and observes the distribution of outcomes that results. Instead of asking "what will happen?" it asks "across all the plausible ways this could go, what range of outcomes should we expect — and how often?"

The name comes from the Monte Carlo casino: the method was formalised by Stanislaw Ulam in the 1940s when he was thinking about card games during convalescence. Neumann and Oppenheimer then used it in nuclear weapons design. Now it lives in every serious financial model, engineering simulation, and — once you understand it — in your head every time you forecast revenue.

The core idea is straightforward: 1. Define your inputs as distributions, not single numbers (e.g., "new clients per month: somewhere between 1 and 4, most likely 2") 2. Draw a random value from each input distribution 3. Compute the output (e.g., MRR at month 12) 4. Repeat steps 2–3 thousands of times 5. Look at the resulting distribution of outputs — the median, the 10th percentile (bad case), the 90th percentile (good case)

Business example: The Kiln wants to forecast whether it hits €100k MRR by month 12. Instead of building one optimistic spreadsheet, model three uncertain inputs:

- New clients per month: uniform distribution between 1 and 4 - Average contract value (ACV): normally distributed, mean €4,000/mo, standard deviation €1,000 - Monthly churn rate: between 2% and 8%, most likely 4%

A simple month-by-month model: MRR(t+1) = MRR(t) × (1 − churn) + new_clients × ACV

Run this 10,000 times. You might find: - Median outcome at month 12: €72,000 MRR - 90th percentile (good run): €118,000 MRR - 10th percentile (bad run): €38,000 MRR

This tells you something a single spreadsheet never can: hitting €100k by month 12 is a real possibility, but the median path doesn't get you there — you need better-than-median performance on at least two of the three inputs.

Insight: The point of Monte Carlo is not to produce a precise forecast — it is to understand the shape of your uncertainty. Most founders build one revenue model and call it a plan. Monte Carlo forces you to admit that each input is a range, not a number, and shows you which input has the most leverage on the outcome. Typically, in a services business: ACV has more variance impact than new client volume, and churn has the most catastrophic tail risk. The simulation makes this visible.

It also cures false precision. A plan that says "we'll hit €100k by October" is a wish. A simulation that says "we hit €100k by October in 31% of scenarios, and in 68% of those scenarios we needed ACV above €4,500" is a strategy.

Today's exercise: Build — or sketch on paper — a three-input Monte Carlo for The Kiln's next six months:

1. Estimate a range (low / most likely / high) for new clients signed per month 2. Estimate a range for average monthly contract value 3. Estimate a range for monthly churn rate

If you have access to Python, Excel, or even a basic spreadsheet, run at least 100 iterations by sampling randomly from those ranges and computing end-of-month MRR each time. If you are doing this by hand, run five distinct scenarios (pessimistic, bad, base, good, optimistic) using the low/mid/high combinations.

Ask: in what percentage of your scenarios do you hit €100k MRR within six months? What single input change moves that percentage the most? That input is your highest-leverage variable — and it deserves disproportionate attention this week.

Next: Markov Chains.

item.title: DLE 2026-05-20
item.description:
1. The Funny One

"Conditional probability: the only branch of mathematics specifically designed to explain why your confidence is wrong in a very precise way."

Use when opening any conversation about data-driven decision making, or when a client insists their gut feel is "basically always right."

2. Business Insight

A — Bezos (Amazon Letters): Working Backwards, Not Skills-Forward. The skills-forward trap is building what you already know how to deliver, then hunting for someone who needs it. Working backwards means starting with what the client actually needs to hit their number — even if it requires building capabilities you don't yet have. At The Kiln, the question isn't "how do we sell more Clay infrastructure?" — it's "what does this specific ICP need to get to their first 50 qualified meetings?" The answer shapes the offer, not the other way around.

B — Collins (Good to Great): The Hedgehog Beats the Fox. The fox knows many things; the hedgehog knows one big thing. Hedgehog companies don't chase adjacencies until they've drilled so deep into their one thing that the answer becomes obvious. The Kiln's "one big thing" — GTM infrastructure that compounds — is the place to drill, not expand away from. Every new service line is a fox move until the hedgehog concept is unassailable.

3. Deep Line

"The map is not the territory." — Alfred Korzybski

Your sales deck, your ICP hypothesis, your funnel model — they are maps. The territory is the messy, conditional, context-dependent reality of what actually causes a prospect to buy. Update the map when the territory contradicts it. Most people redraw the territory to fit the map.

4. Thought Principle: The Base Rate Neglect

People systematically ignore background frequencies when making predictions and decisions — they fixate on the vivid, specific story in front of them and forget to ask "how often does this type of thing actually work out?" A founder hears one warm intro that closed into a €50k deal and rebuilds their entire GTM around warm intros, ignoring that their base rate on intros is one-in-twenty.

Kiln application: Before doubling down on any channel or tactic because of a recent win, ask: what is the actual base rate across all attempts? One spectacular result is a data point, not a distribution. Conditional probability forces you to condition on the relevant reference class — not just on the last thing that worked.

5. New Words & Terms

Posterior probability — in Bayesian reasoning, the updated probability of a hypothesis after incorporating new evidence; what you believe after you've seen the data. "Your posterior probability that this ICP converts should change every time you run a new sequence — if it doesn't, you're not doing Bayesian updating, you're just confirming whatever you already thought."

Conjunction fallacy — the cognitive error of judging a specific, detailed scenario as more probable than a broader, less-specific one; made famous by Kahneman's "Linda the bank teller" experiment. "The conjunction fallacy is why a hyper-specific pitch deck feels more persuasive than an accurate one — detail creates false confidence."

Actuarial thinking — reasoning from aggregate statistical tables and population-level data rather than individual case characteristics; the method used by insurance underwriters. "Most founders do narrative thinking when they should be doing actuarial thinking — your last success story is not a strategy, it's an anecdote."

6. Stoic Closer

"He who is brave is free." — Seneca

Courage is not the absence of uncertainty — it is making the decision anyway, with incomplete information, and owning the consequences.

7. Daily Math: Conditional Probability

Concept: Conditional probability asks: given that we know something has already occurred, what is the probability that something else is true? Written formally as P(A|B) — "the probability of A, given B." It sounds simple but it is devastatingly counterintuitive in practice. The key formula is Bayes' Rule:

P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B)

Where: - P(A) is your prior — what you believed before seeing evidence - P(B|A) is the likelihood — how probable is the evidence if your hypothesis is true - P(B) is the marginal probability — how likely is the evidence overall - P(A|B) is your posterior — your updated belief after seeing the evidence

The most common mistake: confusing P(A|B) with P(B|A). These are not the same number. A medical test that is 95% accurate does not mean a positive result means you have the disease with 95% probability — if the disease is rare (low base rate), most positives will still be false positives.

Business example: Suppose The Kiln runs outbound to Series B SaaS companies. From experience: - 20% of your outbound targets are genuinely a strong ICP fit (P(Good ICP) = 0.20) - When a prospect IS a strong fit, they reply 30% of the time (P(Reply | Good ICP) = 0.30) - When a prospect is NOT a strong fit, they reply 5% of the time (P(Reply | Bad ICP) = 0.05)

A prospect replies to your sequence. What is the probability they are actually a good ICP fit?

P(Good ICP | Reply) = P(Reply | Good ICP) × P(Good ICP) / P(Reply)

First, calculate P(Reply): P(Reply) = P(Reply | Good ICP) × P(Good ICP) + P(Reply | Bad ICP) × P(Bad ICP) P(Reply) = (0.30 × 0.20) + (0.05 × 0.80) P(Reply) = 0.06 + 0.04 = 0.10

Now apply Bayes: P(Good ICP | Reply) = (0.30 × 0.20) / 0.10 = 0.06 / 0.10 = 0.60

So: a reply lifts your confidence that someone is a genuine fit from 20% to 60%. That is the value of evidence. But notice it is not 100% — nearly 4 in 10 replies still come from bad-fit prospects. Your qualification call is doing real work.

Insight: Most founders treat any reply as a hot lead. Conditional probability tells you exactly how much a signal updates your belief — and it's almost never as much as your gut wants it to be. The more you improve your targeting (raising the base rate P(Good ICP)), the more valuable each signal becomes. Poor targeting doesn't just waste effort on outreach — it degrades the diagnostic value of every response you get.

Today's exercise: Estimate three numbers from your actual data or your best honest guess: 1. What percentage of your outbound list is genuinely strong ICP? (Your prior) 2. What percentage of strong-fit prospects reply when you reach them? 3. What percentage of weak-fit prospects reply?

Run the Bayes calculation. How much does a reply actually update your confidence in fit? Now ask: what would have the bigger effect on that posterior — doubling your reply rate through better copy, or doubling your base rate through tighter targeting? The math will almost certainly tell you targeting is the higher-leverage lever.

Next: Monte Carlo.

item.title: DLE 2026-05-19
item.description:
1. The Funny One

"Everyone says 'work smarter, not harder.' Nobody ever explains what smart looks like. So we all just work harder while nodding along."

Use when opening a talk about systems vs. hustle, or when a client admits their team is "maxed out" before you've even diagnosed why.

2. Business Insight

A — Andreessen (pmarca): The Market Pulls. When you have PMF, customers drag the product out of you — you don't push it onto them. The Kiln diagnostic: are inbound leads arriving half-sold, or are you convincing everyone from scratch? If it's the latter, the positioning needs work before the sequencing does.

B — Collins (Good to Great): Packard's Law. A company should limit its growth based on its ability to attract enough of the right people. The temptation at $20k MRR is to take every client and hire fast to cover them. That's exactly how you build something you'll spend a year un-building.

3. Deep Line

"Poor is the apprentice who does not surpass his Master." — Leonardo da Vinci (via Greene)

The goal of every system you build at The Kiln isn't just to deliver — it's to become so internalized that it operates without you. The day a junior operator runs a campaign better than you designed it is a good day, not a threat.

4. Thought Principle: The Vuja De Effect (Grant)

Deja vu is seeing something new and feeling like you've seen it before. Vuja de is the reverse — looking at something utterly familiar with genuinely fresh eyes. Warby Parker happened because someone finally asked why glasses cost more than a smartphone after decades of wearing them.

Kiln application: Look at your clients' existing GTM stack the way a first-principles thinker would. The most valuable insight you can deliver is often hiding inside the most obvious default they've stopped questioning.

5. New Words & Terms

Oligarchy (iron law of, Michels) — the structural tendency of any organization, no matter how democratic its founding, to drift toward rule by a small coordinating elite. "The iron law of oligarchy is why every 'flat' agency has two people who actually decide everything — find them before you pitch the room."

Sinecure — a position that requires little or no work but provides a salary or other benefit; historically, a church office with income but no duties. "Half the VP titles at enterprise companies are sinecures — the actual buying decision lives two levels below."

Aperçu — a brief remark or observation that cuts directly to the essential point; a flash of insight. "The best DLE entries aren't summaries — they're aperçus. One sentence that reframes everything."

6. Stoic Closer

"Do not indulge in long discussions about what a good man should be. Be one." — Marcus Aurelius

The shortest distance between who you are and who you intend to be is the next action you take.

7. Daily Math: Pareto Distribution

Concept: The Pareto Distribution (also called the power law or 80/20 rule) is not a symmetric bell curve — it is a heavily skewed distribution where a small minority of inputs produce the vast majority of outputs. Unlike a normal distribution, the Pareto has no meaningful "average" to regress toward; the top values are so extreme they dwarf everything else. Formally: roughly 20% of causes produce 80% of effects — but the ratio compounds. The top 20% of your top 20% (i.e., 4% of inputs) often produce 64% of outputs.

Business example: At The Kiln, this almost certainly holds. A small number of outbound sequences produce the majority of booked meetings. A small number of clients produce the majority of revenue and referrals. A small number of LinkedIn posts produce the majority of inbound leads. The trap is treating all inputs as roughly equal because they look similar on a spreadsheet.

Insight: The critical move with a Pareto Distribution is not to improve the bottom 80% — that's a waste of leverage. The move is to ruthlessly identify what the top 20% have in common, and do more of exactly that. Fixing the losers rarely beats doubling down on the winners.

Today's exercise: Take your last 20 outbound touchpoints, content pieces, or client conversations. Rank them by outcome (reply rate, meeting booked, deal progressed). Do the top 4 (20%) account for roughly 64–80% of your total results? What do those top 4 have in common — format, personalization level, time of day, ICP match, offer framing? That pattern is your actual playbook. Everything else is noise you've been treating as signal.

Next: Conditional Probability.

item.title: DLE 2026-05-11
item.description:
1. The Funny One

"People ask me what The Kiln does and I say 'we help companies find people who want to talk to them' and they say 'so... marketing?' and I die a little inside."

2. Business Insight

A — Thiel: Distribution IS the Product. Most startups die from distribution failure, not product failure. The Kiln solves the most common cause of startup death.

B — Cialdini: Foot-in-the-Door. Small commitments change self-image. Free audits and quick wins aren't charity — they're commitment devices. 76% vs 17% compliance.

3. Deep Line

"It is easier to cope with a bad conscience than with a bad reputation." — Nietzsche

4. Thought Principle: The Sarick Effect (Grant)

Lead with your biggest flaws when pitching skeptical audiences. It disarms skepticism and increases persuasion. Rufus Griscom sold Babble to Disney for $40M after a slide titled "Here's Why You Should Not Buy Babble."

5. New Words & Terms

Convexity — Limited downside, uncapped upside. Only take convex bets.

Overton Window — The range of acceptable ideas in public discourse. Position yourself where the window is moving.

Praxis — The integration of theory and practice. Not just knowing, but doing informed by knowing.

6. Stoic Closer

"First say to yourself what you would be; and then do what you have to do." — Epictetus

7. Daily Math: Bayes' Theorem

P(A|B) = P(B|A) × P(A) / P(B). Update beliefs when new evidence arrives. Anchor on the base rate first, then adjust. Your gut skips base rates — Bayes doesn't.
